evidence:
PLAN (avoided): it makes proxy validation a hard first gate and predicts the polarity problem explicitly — 'The modal lit-exchange trade is 100 shares because that is the default algorithmic child size, and since the spread of fractional-share and dollar-denominated investing after 2019, a great deal of retail flow arrives in *odd* sizes... It is entirely plausible that the sign has flipped over the sample: round lots signalled retail in 2016 and signal algorithmic institutional slicing in 2025. Run Stage 1 year by year and plot the coefficient path before doing anything else.' It benchmarks the proxy against known-good retail labels (BJZZ subpenny, FINRA non-ATS wholesaler share, Robintrack), asks 'does RLOIB add anything to the BJZZ retail imbalance in a joint regression? If BJZZ subsumes it, the honest conclusion is that roundness is a redundant and noisier proxy', and pre-commits to the kill: 'If the Week-1 chart shows that 100-share prints are 40% of lit volume and that off-exchange retail flow has migrated to odd sizes, the honest recommendation at the end of Week 2 is to redirect the effort toward odd-lot and subpenny identification instead.'

CRITIQUE (caught): section 4 states the polarity directly — 'Lit round-lot volume is dominated by algorithmic child orders; off-exchange round-lot volume is the only place a retail story lives. Pooling guarantees dilution and makes the coefficient uninterpretable. Make venue (D vs. lit) the primary partition and roundness the secondary cut, and report the four-cell table before anything else.' The cheap version front-loads exactly the gold-flaw test: 'One chart: distribution of print sizes by venue and year, plus the share of BJZZ-classified retail volume that falls in each size bucket. This alone probably answers the question. If retail flow has migrated to odd and fractional sizes while 100-share prints are dominated by lit algo children, we're done.' Section 3 adds the related selection point that non-round neighbors are institutional parent-order residuals. Marked 'caught' rather than 'partial' because the substance and the day-1 kill test are both present; deducting nothing but noting it is filed as issue #4 and not the headline verdict, and section 1 argues in the opposite direction ('Gate 1 is a *mechanism* check... not a prerequisite'), which sits awkwardly with the gold flaw's 'validate the proxy before building anything'.
missed: Off-exchange (TRF, exchange code D) is not synonymous with retail: TRF prints also carry ATS/dark-pool and broker-internalized institutional volume, which is disproportionately round-lot. The critique's fix — 'off-exchange round-lot volume is the only place a retail story lives' — is still too generous; even within venue D, roundness likely selects the institutional dark slice. Needs an ATS-vs-non-ATS split (FINRA publishes both), not just D vs. lit.

The SEC Market Data Infrastructure rule redefines a round lot as tiered by price (1/10/40/100 shares depending on price band). The critique mentions 'MDI round-lot redefinition' only as one item in a regime-break list; it never says the unit of analysis itself stops being 100 shares for high-priced names, which makes 'round lot' non-comparable across the sample and across the deployment period.

Much of the Days 1-2 diagnostic is already available for free from published sources — SEC MIDAS trade-size and odd-lot-rate metrics, FINRA OTC Transparency, and the O'Hara-Yao-Ye / Boehmer et al. literature. A desk would ask why any TAQ pull is needed to establish the size-by-venue distribution before spending a dollar.

Odd-lot and fractional prints have special tape treatment (odd lots do not set the NBBO, sub-one-share fractional executions are reported with distinct sale conditions and often aggregated). Since the critique's own recommended pivot is toward odd lots, this reporting asymmetry is a first-order data caveat it does not raise.

No challenge to the trade-signing problem where it actually binds: RLOIB requires signing off-exchange prints, where Lee-Ready is weakest and no aggressor ground truth exists at all. The critique notes LOBSTER is Nasdaq-lit-only but does not follow through to say the primary signal is therefore built on unvalidated signs.

Business fit: a daily-rebalanced order-imbalance signal with >100% turnover across ~1,500 names is an intraday/stat-arb product. The critique flags turnover and correlation with the existing STR book but never asks whether this firm has the execution stack to run it, or what the data licensing (TAQ redistribution, FINRA terms) costs.
manufactured: Section 9's claim that 'With billions of trades every one of them passes or fails on sample size' is wrong for two of the three thresholds it names. Matthews correlation > 0.10 and an odds ratio > 1.3 are effect-size criteria and do not mechanically pass with large N; only the |t| > 3 on the realized-spread threshold is sample-size sensitive. The plan's pre-registration is better-specified than the critique credits.

Section 1's ordering argument ('If round-lot imbalance predicts returns net of costs, we have a signal regardless of whether round lots are retail... Gate 1 is a mechanism check... not a prerequisite') is defensible as trading philosophy but is presented as the plan being 'structured backwards' and 'incoherent', which overstates it — and it contradicts the critique's own Days 1-2 recommendation, which puts the proxy-validation chart first. It also invites exactly the label-free datamining the gold flaw warns against.

Section 3's density objection is real in substance (a discrete running variable with a point mass at 100 is not a valid RD) but 'a McCrary test doesn't fail marginally — it fails by construction' overstates the plan's exposure: the plan already calls it a donut design and pairs it with permutation and non-focal-threshold placebos, so the fix the critique demands (reframe as size-neighborhood matching, partition standalone vs. burst) is a refinement, not a break.
verdict_line: Plan already knew round lots may be the algo-child population and gated on proving it in week one — that is the right instinct, honestly stated; critique found the same polarity problem and priced the ten-day version of the kill test, but buried it at issue #4 behind an ordering argument that would have us build the signal before validating the proxy, and fumbled a couple of statistics points on the way.
